idiom_name: mock provider records interactions into a contract file; the provider replays each interaction under a declared provider state
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: write the consumer's test against its own client class, pointed at a local mock provider that validates the outgoing request and serves the declared response, and let the passing run emit the contract (one entry per interaction, with matching rules and the provider state it needs). On the provider side, replay each interaction in isolation - set up the named state, issue the recorded request against the running provider, and match status, headers and body using the recorded rules - then publish the result and use it to decide whether a given consumer version may be deployed against a given provider version. Without a library the mock server, contract writer and verifier are hand-built; the contract format is portable across all implementations.
code_sketch:
consumer test: declare interaction -> mock provider validates the client's request
                -> interactions serialized to a contract file
contract:       { consumer, provider, interactions[], provider states, matching rules }
provider test:  for each interaction: set up provider state, replay request, match response
release gate:   may consumer-version x be deployed against provider-version y?
pitfalls: Skipping the request validation in the mock turns the test into a stub: the contract then records what you hoped the client sends, not what it sends.
Chaining write-then-read in one test is impossible by design - interactions verify in isolation, so a misnamed field can be silently ignored by the provider.
Contracts that are never verified by the provider are documentation with a version number; wire the verification into the provider build or drop the contract.
